items.title: What Constant Surveillance Is Doing to Children
items.description: Illustrations by Miguel Porlan This article was featured in the One Story to Read Today newsletter. Sign up for it here. No one warned me, when I became a parent, about all the apps that would colonize my phone: the app for the baby monitor where I could gaze at my daughter, even when my husband and I finally had a night out. The app for the Snoo smart bassinet we rented in bleary-eyed desperation, which logged her sleep by the minute. The app where I logged her sleep manually because the Snoo was not accurate enough. And still, I remember thinking that I had been quite restrained. I mean, I didn’t buy the $299 Owlet smart sock, which would send her pulse rate and oxygen saturation directly to my phone, or the $290 Nanit monitor, which would track her every breath. Our day care did not have a livestream—see? restraint ⁠—but that is indeed a service some now offer. Preschool required its own app, though, as did summer camp. Soon my phone began pinging with messages about playground spats and injuries as minor as paper cuts. As I write this, I’ve learned that my daughter woke from her nap at 2:17 p.m. The panopticon doesn’t end with babies and toddlers. Parents with children older than mine tell me they obsess over grades, which are updated instantly with each new assignment or quiz. They watch their kids via the camera on their Ring doorbell; they monitor text messages. They scrutinize daily photos from sleepaway camp—once a time of complete disconnection—for evidence of sunburns or social ostracism. Why is he standing apart from everyone else? Why isn’t he smiling? But most of all, parents track their kids everywhere they go. Location tracking might start, for younger kids, with an AirTag slipped into a backpack, jacket, or shoe. (Skechers now makes shoes with a dedicated compartment in the sole.) For kids old enough to have their own smartwatch or phone, the GPS is built right in—and so parents keep tracking them into adolescence and even beyond. Three-quarters of parents with teenagers ages 14 to 17 had access to their kids’ location data, according to one study. [ From the April 2014 issue: Hanna Rosin on the overprotected kid ] Even among college students, one-third were being tracked by their parents, according to another study, conducted in 2021 by Michaeline Jensen, a psychologist at the University of North Carolina at Greensboro. Five years later, Jensen says, that number is even higher: More than half of college students are being tracked, per her unpublished data. In her own lab, she’s learned that even her graduate students continue to be tracked; she told me about one student, 29, who recently defended her dissertation but whose mom still checks—and calls about—her location. If watching your kid’s real-time location isn’t enough, there is Life360, a tracking app that allows parents to review up to 30 days of time-stamped location history, monitor driving to make sure their kids stay within the speed limit, and get alerts when they arrive at or leave saved locations, such as home, school, and, yes, a college dorm. “Holy sh—,” a psychologist who studies kids’ resilience started to say when I described the app to him. But a college psychiatrist whose patients include undergrads needed no introduction to Life360. “Students spend so much time complaining to me about that thing,” she said. The app has 102 million active monthly users and counting. What is all of this tracking doing to us? Lately, I have been posing a version of this question to child-development experts as well as parents and teens themselves. “It’s funny,” Kaitlyn Burnell, a psychologist at UNC Chapel Hill who has studied digital tracking, remarked when I asked her the question. “As you’re saying that, I literally got a notification from my 1-year-old’s day care saying that she ate a graham cracker.” I have not yet found a randomized controlled trial parsing the effects of parental notifications about graham crackers—nor, to be more serious, are there any long-term data on outcomes for parents who use these apps to monitor their babies from birth. But while it’s hard to argue that newborns are suffering from overattentive parenting, developmental psychology does suggest that constant monitoring eventually becomes unhealthy. One of the primary developmental tasks of adolescence, Burnell told me, is achieving a measure of independence. “If you have this metaphorical umbilical cord,” she asked, “is that sense of independence going to be adequately developed?” [ From the May 2020 issue: Kate Julian on childhood in an anxious age ] The more I probed what constant monitoring is doing to kids, the more I also started to wonder what it is doing to parents, on the other end of the umbilical cord. Our phones promise us a kind of omniscience from the moment a kid is born. Even when we are physically apart, we remain digitally tethered. But as parents, we are supposed to undergo our own transformation as our children grow, relinquishing the knowledge and control we once held. “That’s an important developmental task for parents too,” Burnell said. And here, we parents might be failing ourselves. We are certainly not thriving. In 2024, the U.S. surgeon general issued a public-health advisory about the mental health of parents, echoing a similar advisory about youth mental health three years earlier. In a national survey in which 18 percent of teens reported anxiety, so did 18 percent of parents. For all the recent concern about a crisis in teen mental health, parents are clearly struggling too. I think of the immortal words of my 3-year-old this morning: “Calm down, Mom!” When Maureen Paschal, a college counselor in North Carolina, sent her daughter off to college a few years ago, she was promptly invited to join a group chat for moms of the girls living on the same floor. The moms, she recalls, tracked their daughters’ location during sorority rush, watching as they moved from house to house. But the incident that stuck in her mind came one fall morning, when a mom messaged the group chat that her daughter was still in her dorm room. She had a math test in 10 minutes. Could someone ask their kid to go knock on her door? Miguel Porlan “I just was like, This is too much. It’s just too much ,” Paschal told me. But not everyone thought so. Another mom soon replied: My daughter is on her way. In a sense, the scene that Paschal described was nothing new. Helicopter parenting came into popular use some 20 years ago, and articles about parents who trail their kids, metaphorically and literally, on campus still drop every fall, like acorns from an oak tree. But what stood out to me about this anecdote were all the phones—and how frictionless they make it to indulge every parental anxiety that pops in your head. [ Read: Russell Shaw’s Raising Resilient Children newsletter ] One step leads so easily to another: If you’re invited to a group chat for parents, why not join? If you can see where your kid is on campus, why not look? If they’re not where they are supposed to be, why not say something? All it takes is a few taps on your phone, which you pull out reflexively anyway whenever you sit on the couch. Back in the dumbphone era, my own mother could not have spent all day messaging the moms of my freshman dormmates even if she’d wanted to. And I feel quite confident that zero of my teenage friends’ parents tracked their location—again, because they couldn’t, at least not without an alarming amount of effort. Then, in 2015, Apple made a software change that may have done more to normalize location tracking than anything else: The company began shipping iPhones preloaded with Find My Friends, allowing people to share their location with one another. As the name implies, the app was not originally created for families , but it’s since become a default option for parents tracking their kids. (The app merged with Find My iPhone in 2019 to become just Find My.) Life360, which launched in 2008 after one of its founders saw families trying to find one another in Hurricane Katrina’s chaotic aftermath, has taken off in recent years too. Its monthly active users have quadrupled since 2020, with revenue totaling almost half a billion dollars last year. These are the two most popular location-tracking apps. Both are effortless to use. When I first talked with teens and young adults about location tracking, I would start by asking when their parents began tracking them. I soon realized that this was like asking when they began eating solid foods. Like, always? For many kids, location tracking came automatically with their first smartwatch or phone, without much ado. For many parents, too, location tracking eased into their lives because it was available. “Once we had that tool,” a mom of four told me, “it felt like we were irresponsible if we didn’t use it.” I remember this feeling as well, when I first saw neighborhood moms discussing how to attach an AirTag to a 3-year-old. Wait, was I supposed to be doing that? Had I been cavalier—irresponsible—by sending my kid off to preschool without one? Let’s first say this: Location tracking is so useful! Convenience and coordinating logistics are the main reasons cited by about a third of parents who use it, according to preliminary data collected by William Pelham III, a UC San Diego psychologist who last year began a nearly 1,000-family study about location tracking during adolescence. Pelham, who came to this topic after studying substance use and delinquency in teens, told me his original interviews were geared toward asking about behaviors such as breaking curfew, having sex, and taking drugs. The third parent who came in tried to stop the interview, telling the researchers, “You guys don’t get it. I use these apps purely for logistics. I use it to figure out when I’m picking him up at high school: Is he at the east door or the west door? ” For parents who use location tracking only like this, it’s not that complicated⁠—no need to overthink it. But safety is another big motivation, cited as the primary reason by 40 percent of parents in Pelham’s data. And Pelham is interested in how parents ensure safety through location tracking: “What is the behavior? Does that mean checking every single day?” Multiple times a day? Calling—or even driving over if the parent sees something they don’t like? Faith, a recent college graduate, told me her mom watched her closely on Life360 in high school. (I’m using only first or middle names for some of the people I interviewed, so they can speak candidly about their family life.) “She would call me when I’m on the highway, lecturing me about how fast I was going,” she said. “Or there was this one time that I was at a friend’s house and she didn’t recognize the address. And she went to that friend’s house from my location and knocked on the door.” It was embarrassing, Faith said, but her friend wasn’t particularly shocked; this kind of thing happens when everyone is being tracked. When the app glitched, as it sometimes does, her mom would drive out to the random location she saw on Life360. Faith’s relationship with her mom was rocky to start with in high school, which made Faith closed off, which made her mom more dependent on Life360, which made Faith feel even less trusted—a downward spiral that many experts I spoke with warned about. The handful of studies on location tracking of teens have found mixed or only very small effects on the teen-parent relationship, though they also have not probed too deeply into how the parents use it. (Nor have they, altogether, found a consistent relationship between tracking and socioeconomic class.) In general, the studies don’t distinguish between the parent who looks at their teen’s location only during pickup and the parent driving out to any unknown location on Life360. Many parents who use location tracking, I suspect, fall somewhere between these two extremes. Watching their kid’s location dot is not about control so much as peace of mind. The apps offer a “perception of safety,” Gregory Chase, who studied location tracking of teens as a Ph.D. student in Jensen’s lab at UNC Greensboro, told me. He elaborated on the difference: “When you know someone’s location, you don’t necessarily know who they’re with or what kind of behavior they could be engaging in.” You can see your son in his dorm room and not know he’s binge drinking; you can see your daughter at a friend’s and not know about a sexual assault, the majority of which are perpetrated by someone known to the victim. But at least you can rule out your kid lying in a ditch somewhere? A persistent theme in my conversations, and in conversations that experts say they have with parents, is the sense that the world has become more dangerous and too many risks lurk out there. This is not borne out in the statistics: In just about every way, teenagers are living safer lives than ever. They are not only less likely to be victims of violence than in the 1990s, when crime peaked; they are also less likely to smoke, drink, use hard drugs, or get pregnant. The rates of all these behaviors have plummeted by more than half. “There’s some kind of risk-taking dimension that’s definitely down in teens,” Pelham said. The pendulum swing toward safety has real benefits, but it may have costs too. Teenagers today are also less likely to get a job, go on a date, or drive—all of which involve some small but tangible risk or uncertainty in the physical world. Their lives have turned inward, and when they do venture out, they’re tracked. By coincidence or not, the rates of depression and anxiety in teenagers have steadily increased. These trends “feel intuitively connected, right?” Pelham said. He is careful to acknowledge that this observation is more inference than empirical fact. The cause of the teen mental-health crisis is a topic of debate, much of it recently centered on the role of social media. But it’s hard to imagine that a diminished tolerance for risk and uncertainty in teenagers is not affecting their well-being. And perhaps parents feel it on some level too, because even those who closely track their kids spoke to me with evident nostalgia about their own freer, wilder youth—the opposite of what they are giving their children. “A lot of parents today are just super hypocritical,” Henry Stuart, a college junior, told me. His dad still tracks him. “This is the same generation that talks all the time about Oh, it was so great in the ’80s; like, we could just ride our bikes all around the neighborhood, and, you know, we would come home when the sun goes down ,” Stuart said. “But then these are the same parents that are on Life360, stalking their kids and watching their every move.” Miguel Porlan Thomas Parker, a dad of two and stepdad of four, encountered location tracking before he had teens of his own. (He doesn’t track but his ex-wife does.) He had used a version of it, called Blue Force Tracking, while deployed in the military. “Everybody hated it,” he told me. Well, clarified Parker, now a mental-health counselor in Arkansas, “we loved it, in that if we were ambushed or something and we needed help, they could tell exactly where we were—but it also turned into a nanny state. Like, You’re only supposed to be driving 30 and you’re driving 35. You have to slow down .” Even in a war zone, it could be too much. Russell Shaw told me a story about getting lost on a family vacation when he was 7 years old. He had gone to a video arcade with his older brother, who left first, after asking if Shaw knew the way back to the motel. “I said, ‘Uh huh.’ ” His brother left. “Then I walked out of the place and I had no idea where to go.” What next? This was the 1970s: no cellphones, no GPS. In truth, he was not far, perhaps a block away, but in his little-kid brain, he was utterly, deeply lost. He wandered. He eventually found an adult, who took him to the police, who drove him around until he spotted his parents walking down the street in search of him. “It sucked at the time,” he said, “and then the next time something like that happened, I thought, Oh, I can get through this .” In his telling some half a century later, this story is not about the traumatic experience of getting lost but about how his younger self overcame it. What if his parents had been able to immediately swoop in because they saw his coordinates on their phone? There would have been no getting lost, no “it sucked,” but also no eventual triumph. Shaw, who until recently was the head of Georgetown Day School, in Washington, D.C., has written a newsletter for The Atlantic about raising resilient kids and is working on a book about the topic. He wonders what all of this location tracking means for kids’ resilience. “If we are being tracked or surveilled, and there is a ubiquitous sense that we can be rescued, are we not fully internalizing that sense of our own capacity?” he said. “And ultimately, there will come a time when we do need to stand on our own two feet.” Shaw’s story of getting lost stayed with me because I did, in fact, hear the inverted version from parents who track their kids. The modern tale goes something like this: A teen makes a mistake while driving or taking the subway; in a panic, they call their parents, who look up their location and coach them back to where they need to be—thank goodness for tracking. One parent who recounted such a scenario is Louise Barkhuus, who actually studies location tracking as part of her research at NYU on human-computer interaction. She has been interested in the topic since 2003; early on, she found it difficult to recruit volunteers willing to install location-tracking apps, so unusual—even invasive—was the technology back then. (These days, she says, “it’s so easy.”) In her own life, when Barkhuus’s daughter first started taking the subway alone, she kept a close eye on her location, and would text if the app showed her on a train going in the wrong direction. Several times, her daughter called her mom lost, asking where to go. I wasn’t sure, at first, how Barkhuus felt about micromanaging her daughter’s subway rides. But when I told her about Shaw’s story of getting lost at 7, and his worry that parents are no longer giving kids the opportunity to navigate these situations on their own, she responded, “I think it’s completely correct.” In the moment, though, what mother is going to hang up on her panicking daughter? “We’re oversurveilling our children in a way that’s not necessary,” Barkhuus said, “but I don’t know how to take it away.” Barkhuus’s own research has chronicled how location tracking has become normalized, even among kids themselves. Sure, teens and young adults with particularly intrusive parents resent the stalking—some have learned to get around tracking, by tinkering with the settings or leaving their phone behind in a friend’s mailbox—but many find reassurance in being tracked. (They are also all sharing their location with their friends.) Some of the college students she interviewed actually initiated it with their less tech-savvy parents. They’ve internalized the idea that they need it. Even Faith, who hated her mom’s use of Life360, nevertheless said she understood the underlying motivation: “The world was getting more dangerous and it’s just a safety thing, which I agree with fully.” Where might teenagers be hearing that the world is now so dangerous, other than from their parents? Over the past half century, the norms of parenting have veered hard toward safetyism. My colleague Hanna Rosin wrote about this shift in her 2014 Atlantic article “ The Overprotected Kid, ” in which she observed that the independence of her own childhood seemed unbelievable a generation later. From 1971 to 2010, in one large U.K. study, the percentage of parents who allowed their 7- and 8-year-olds to walk home from school alone fell from 80 percent to 6 percent. Children absorb the sense that danger can lurk around every street corner, because it’s what their parents taught them. Perhaps it shouldn’t come as a surprise that when researchers look at the risk factors for anxiety in children, one of the strongest is having an anxious parent; genetics plays a role, but so does parenting. Barkhuus told me another story, about a time she took the train on her own as a girl of 12. She grew up in Denmark in the ’80s, but the freedom with which she remembers moving through the world is not so different from what Americans of the same generation recall. One day, there was a big train accident. Barkhuus was fine, but the trains were delayed on the way home, and she was an hour late to her brother’s birthday party. I imagined how this would play out in 2026, if a 12-year-old spent an hour unaccounted for: Mom calling, calling, calling; checking the news and seeing that there was a train accident; calling; fearing the worst; calling, calling, calling until her kid finally showed up or called back. When Barkhuus got home, she remembers, her mom had simply assumed that her daughter was off doing her thing. She was annoyed, initially, at Barkhuus’s tardiness to the party, but she had not constructed a whole scary scenario in her head. “She didn’t think about an accident. She wasn’t worried.” Without the expectation of being constantly connected, her mother had simply gone on with the birthday party. She trusted that her daughter would eventually show up, and she did. But what if something had happened—outside the video arcade, or on the train? If you, like me, have a tendency to worry, perhaps this shadow of doubt also appeared unbidden in your brain, in which case, boy, do I have a Life360 commercial for you. It opens in a kitchen as a mother sings to her teenage daughter: You are my whole wide world, My heart, my joy, my baby girl. You’ll never know how much I love you! When you’re gone I just think of you … Dying. Her voice drops. The live-action commercial turns into a cartoon enacting her words. Every time you leave my sight, When you drive to school or stay out at night, This is where I go, To the million ways inside my brain In which you could die at any given time. You could bleed out on the street or get stuck in a mine. You could get kidnapped by bandits. Some creep could harvest all your organs and then sell them online. There are a million ways inside my brain In which you could die at any given time. You could be flattened like a pancake by hydraulic machines, Or be sucked into a wood chipper by the leg of your jeans … And so it continues, with more and more outlandish scenarios for a whole minute, as the daughter rolls her eyes. It’s a funny ad, very tongue-in-cheek, I remarked to Lenore Skenazy, who quickly interjected. “You laugh, a little ruefully, but they normalize the idea that catastrophizing—‘worst-first thinking,’ I call it—imagining your kid dead is just the normal,” she said. “And the only way to assuage it is to check, check, check, check your phone.” The commercial ends with the daughter handing her mom a phone installed with Life360. “There,” the daughter says. “No more freaking out.” Just check Life360. Skenazy is one of the foremost public advocates against this need to “check, check, check, check” on your kids, a position she held long before their phones were beaming their location into our pockets. In 2008, as a columnist for The New York Sun , she wrote about leaving her 9-year-old at a Manhattan Bloomingdale’s with a subway map, a MetroCard, and $20 to find his way home alone. He made it, “ecstatic with independence,” she wrote, but her actions provoked such hostile backlash, she was inspired to a new life’s mission. She came out with a book, Free-Range Kids , and a reality-TV show, World’s Worst Mom , where she coaxed overprotective parents to, for example, let their tween daughter use a public bathroom by herself. Skenazy also co-founded the nonprofit Let Grow to promote kids’ independence, along with Daniel Shuchman, a private investor and philanthropist; Jonathan Haidt, a social psychologist best known as the author of the anti-phone treatise The Anxious Generation ; and Peter Gray, an evolutionary psychologist who recently came out with his own book blaming the decline in teen mental health on schools, rather than phones. Let Grow’s founders may disagree on why, but they do all agree that society is squelching kids’ independence—to their detriment. I mention all of this to suggest that, on one hand, Skenazy’s message of child independence has found a receptive audience, at least in certain circles. She is an excellent messenger too, by turns funny and unsparing. Skenazy and her co-founders at Let Grow are frequently featured in magazines such as this one. And parents who inhabit brownstone Brooklyn neighborhoods like mine talk often of aspiring to some flavor of free-range parenting. On the other hand, the past 20 years have been a long, exhausting march toward more parental surveillance—and surveillance in general. Since Free-Range Kids was published, the percentage of parents tracking their kids’ location has risen from approximately zero to 100 percent. (I exaggerate, but not that much.) And as I discovered when I had a baby, the products for monitoring your kids at a young age have multiplied with technological progress. When Skenazy’s kids were small, baby monitors were more or less audio-only affairs. In this age of smart monitors, she said, imagine what monitoring a baby’s every breath does to a parent. “You’re supposed to be holding your own breath to say, ‘Okay, she breathed. [ Gasp. ] She breathed. [ Gasp. ] She breathed. [ Gasp. ] She breathed. [ Gasp. ]’ And so you’re turning regular life into a near disaster that you must be alerted to all the time.” An app like this sells short-term peace of mind, she argued, “but it delivers the opposite. It delivers the impression that your child is only safe because you are in control.” And if hypervigilance is the only way to keep your kid safe, how can you ever stop watching? Today, it’s monitoring your newborn’s every breath; tomorrow, it’ll be physically hovering over your toddler’s every step; in 20 years, it’ll still be tracking their every step, now from afar. Anxiety becomes a form of caring, surveillance a form of love. Most parents agree—in the abstract—that kids need to confront their own challenges and make their own mistakes as they grow up. They need to learn how to ask for help when lost. They need to face the consequences of oversleeping for a math test before they oversleep for a job interview. But when you’re hovering digitally, phone in hand, it is so natural to want to help and so easy to intervene. Miguel Porlan Skenazy argues that the apps deprive parents of the opportunity to develop their own muscles: “There’s no reps of your letting go of your kid, living without knowledge for a little while, and then them returning safe and sound. And you’re realizing, Wow, I don’t have to worry every single second .” Instead we have been trained to check and check again, as if reassurance can be found only on our phones. Perhaps the last person I expected to endorse Skenazy’s views was Chris Hulls, co-founder, executive chairman, and until last year also CEO of Life360. “I really like her,” he told me. “I agree with her on so much.” Hulls grew up in Marin County, California, as a free-range kid himself— very free-range, in fact. At age 11, he told me, he traveled to Kenya on his own, where he lived with the family of an Episcopal priest whom he had recently met. “It was out in the bush with no power, no water, not only no cellphones, but no phones period, so I was completely, completely unfindable.” He could call his parents only on a weekly trip to Nairobi. “If something bad happened, it would have taken probably days for my parents to find out, and I almost got bitten by a puff adder out there,” he said. “That could have killed me.” Hulls didn’t die, obviously, and the experience was a formative one; after high school, he joined the Air Force, then studied business at UC Berkeley, and then founded Life360, which began as a school project after Hurricane Katrina. The early years of running the app were a grind—he lived in a friend’s closet—until it finally took off. Hulls has not chosen the risk-averse path in life. He agrees with Skenazy about the importance of kids’ independence. And he agrees that “safetyism is a thing, and it’s not a good thing.” But in a world where parents are already preoccupied with safety, he argues, Life360 actually grants teenagers more independence, by giving parents the peace of mind to allow activities they otherwise would not. “Absolutely some parents do go over the top,” he said. “But I think the average teen is getting more freedom and autonomy, not less.” Life360’s current CEO, Lauren Antonoff, told me the average user opens the app five times a day; a spokesperson later added that less than 4 percent open it 10 times a day and less than 1 percent more than 20 times a day. Most app usage, Antonoff said, is driven by people managing school pickup and other day-to-day logistics, not monitoring for safety. Safety is core to the company’s business, though. Life360 is a freemium app: Basic location tracking is free, but extra safety functions, such as individual driver reports and additional days of location history, can be unlocked for $9.99 to $24.99 a month. (Like all freemium apps, it is constantly nudging you to upgrade.) Safety “drives a lot of our retention and our revenue,” Hulls told me. So what was the intent of the ad, I asked, where the mom sings about her daughter dying? “I thought it was the opposite of fearmongering,” he said. “It’s making fun of fearmongering.” But perhaps the real genius is that it does both. The ad has been viewed nearly 9 million times on YouTube. Maureen Paschal , the mom who told me about the parent group chat for her daughter’s dorm, recounted that story because she herself understood the impulse to track. “I knew I would be obsessed,” she said, if she had her daughter’s location. Paschal’s solution was to make her husband use the app on his phone. She could ask for her daughter’s location in a real emergency, but by placing a big obstacle—her husband—in the way, she could not check all the time. Other moms (yes, it is mostly moms who track) also told me about how they came to check the apps out of compulsion, habit, or simple longing. When Julie Bohannon-Wyczynski’s daughter went to college, she would open up Life360 every day. “Everything in me wants to check and text her,” she recalls thinking. “I need to let it go.” She found herself similarly obsessed with her younger sons’ grades in their school app, questioning them about any suspicious zeros she saw. “Mom, the teacher has not put in the grades yet,” her sons would say, rolling their eyes. Bohannon-Wyczynski, who is a therapist herself, soon realized that checking whenever she had 10 minutes free at work was not healthy behavior. [ From the July/August 2011 issue: Lori Gottlieb on how to land your kid in therapy ] Indeed, to psychologists, repeatedly checking an app is the opposite of how you’re supposed to deal with anxiety. This behavior is called reassurance seeking. “It is a trap,” Camilo Ortiz, a clinical psychologist on Long Island, told me. “You feel better immediately, and then you need it again.” Or sometimes, you feel worse. Several years ago, Ortiz said, he saw his daughter’s location in the middle of a wooded park during the school day. “I called her and I couldn’t get through to her, and I became panicked,” he said. “I drove home 100 miles an hour because I was convinced she was kidnapped in a park.” (She had actually gone on the subway, and the app had glitched.) “If I were to do it over again, I would track much less.” Recently, Ortiz, who is on Let Grow’s advisory board, started piloting what he calls independence therapy for anxious kids. The therapy has kids brainstorm and carry out a series of activities unsupervised, such as taking the bus or walking to the deli to buy cold cuts. These activities are meant to expose kids to small doses of uncertainty and discomfort in scenarios that are not the direct source of their anxieties. (By analogy, Ortiz pointed to a small study where participants who were treated with exposure therapy to spiders became less fearful of heights too.) One of the first participants, Ortiz said, was a 9-year-old girl who was afraid to sleep in her own bed. She chose to ride the city bus by herself. The girl actually missed her stop, but she found a grown-up, who helped her get off and backtrack the extra blocks home. That night, she slept in her own bed for the first time. “I can’t know for sure, but I think the getting-lost part and realizing, Oh, even if the worst thing happens, I can figure it out was crucial for her in terms of her own sense of self-efficacy,” Ortiz said. Hers is one of four cases that he published in a 2024 study. When Ortiz pitches independence therapy to parents, “the first question is: But I can still track them, right? ” Sure, he tells them, but the ultimate goal is no tracking at all. Just as the therapy teaches kids to tolerate uncertainty and discomfort, it’s meant to teach parents the same. “We think this is a stealth treatment for parents,” he said. Recently, he’s been experimenting with a version of independence therapy for just parents. They meet as a group over Zoom before having their kids carry out a daily unsupervised activity for three weeks. Can treating parents indirectly treat kids? (This basic idea also underlies a more established treatment program called SPACE , or Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions, which has generated enormous interest lately; it teaches parents to stop accommodating their child’s anxieties.) One dad who went through Ortiz’s program last year, whom I’ll call by his middle name, Thomas, told me he had never considered himself anxious. He let his 12-year-old son walk to school and to the park with a friend—albeit while tracking his son’s location and sometimes even following on foot “like a private investigator, just to, I don’t know, make sure they didn’t die.” In therapy, Thomas learned that he was supposed to eventually give up tracking. “Well, that’s insane,” he recalls thinking. “I must know at all times where he is. When he’s 25, I’m going to want to know where he is.” He described that moment as “a turning point when I was like, Oh fuck, I’m just as crazy as all these other parents .” Thomas did stop following his son on foot—but the tracking, well, he hasn’t been able to turn that off yet. Other parents told me about learning to counter not just their own anxieties but those of other adults as well, now that everyone’s unused to seeing children walking around alone. “Are you really going to let Casey go into Walmart by herself?” Darleen Smith remembers her family asking about her 11-year-old daughter. Smith did let her daughter go to Walmart, and also to CVS and the nail salon and a movie and to set up a lemonade stand, which became six or seven lemonade stands. “She lasted, like, three, four hours some days, and she wasn’t complaining at all. That surprised me,” she said. Things didn’t always work out perfectly; her daughter asked neighbors if she could walk their dog and no one took her up on it. But in giving her daughter the space to fail, she also gave her the space to exceed her expectations. Casey made more than $1,000 at her lemonade stands. You don’t need to sign up for independence therapy to let your kid take the bus or walk through Walmart untracked. You can just do it. You can just do things. But the program, I noticed in my conversations, gave parents much-needed permission to break social norms, however uncomfortable that made everyone involved. It almost always went better than they expected. When Courtney Perrone, another parent in the group therapy, started having her 9- and 10-year-old daughters plan dinner and buy groceries by themselves, other parents in her small town realized that their kids could do this too. “It ended up sparking even a little bit more independence, I would say, around the neighborhood,” she told me. “You now have multiple kids at the grocery store by themselves.” And that’s the thing about social norms: We create them, and we can re-create them too. This article appears in the December 2026 print edition with the headline “The Geo-Located Generation.” When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. items.title: Axe Ouaga-Bobo: un accident de la circulation fait six morts sur la RN1
items.description: Un accident de la circulation a fait six morts sur la Route nationale 1 (RN1), l’axe principal reliant les deux capitales, Ouagadougou et Bobo-Dioulasso, dans la nuit du dimanche 8 au lundi 9 novembre 2026, rapporte Sidwaya. Une collision entre deux cars de transport en commun a causé un accident qui fait six morts sur l’axe Ouagadougou et Bobo-Dioulasso dans la nuit du dimanche au lundi 9 novembre 2026 aux environs de la localité de Sabou. Selon le bilan provisoire établi, les six personnes sont décédées sur le coup, en plus de nombreux autres passagers, grièvement blessés qui ont été évacués d'urgence vers les centres de santé de Koudougou et de Sabou par les éléments de la Brigade nationale des Sapeurs-pompiers (BNSP) de Koudougou. Par Wakat Séra L’article Axe Ouaga-Bobo: un accident de la circulation fait six morts sur la RN1 est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .

items.title: Gestion des frontières : changement de cadre
items.description: © Internet Deux projets de texte réorganisent les principales structures nationales du secteur. Le gouvernement annonce des missions renforcées et une composition élargie. Créée en mars 1999, la Direction nationale des Frontières prépare les éléments de la politique nationale dans ce domaine. Elle coordonne également l’action des autorités administratives, des services publics et des organismes qui participent à son application. Le gouvernement reconnaît aujourd’hui un pilotage stratégique insuffisant, ainsi que des faiblesses dans la coordination des acteurs et la mobilisation des ressources. Les projets adoptés le 6 novembre remplacent le cadre d’organisation établi par deux décrets de 1999. Ils prévoient aussi les effectifs nécessaires au fonctionnement de la Direction pendant les cinq prochaines années. Le communiqué ne fournit toutefois ni le nombre de postes concernés, ni leur répartition territoriale, ni les moyens financiers attachés à cette programmation. La publication des textes complets précisera également les éventuelles nouvelles directions internes et les compétences confiées aux services régionaux. La seconde réforme concerne la Commission nationale des Frontières. Instituée en 2003, elle assiste le ministre chargé des Frontières dans la mise en œuvre de la politique nationale. Le projet de décret adopté étend ses missions et ouvre sa composition à d’autres acteurs concernés. Le gouvernement rattache cette évolution aux recommandations des Assises nationales de la Refondation et du Dialogue inter-Maliens. Les frontières relèvent à la fois de l’administration territoriale, de la circulation des personnes, des échanges commerciaux et de la coopération avec les pays voisins. La Direction nationale coordonne les services concernés, tandis que la Commission exerce une fonction de concertation et d’appui au ministre. Les projets adoptés n’annoncent pas la création d’une nouvelle force opérationnelle. Pour l'heure, il n'y a pas encore de poste frontalier supplémentaire, chantier de démarcation ou mécanisme bilatéral précis n’est mentionné dans le communiqué. Ces éléments permettront, après publication, de mesurer les changements perceptibles pour les habitants, les transporteurs et les commerçants des zones frontalières.

items.title: Japoma : le titre foncier en mode loterie d’Etat
items.description: © DR Par un arrêt de la Cour suprême, l’État vient d’effacer d’un trait de plume le titre foncier n°34535/W de la collectivité de Japoma-Bakoko et près de 800 titres parcellaires. 278 hectares rayés, des familles jetées dans l’angoisse. Il faut le lire pour le croire. Le titre foncier n°34535/W, immatriculé le 1er avril 2005 au nom de la collectivité villageoise de Japoma-Bakoko, est annulé « avec toutes les conséquences de droit ». Avec lui, le n°37711/W et leurs démembrements. C’est la Chambre administrative de la Cour suprême qui l’a décidé, par l’arrêt n°079/P/FD/2025 du 4 juin 2025, rendu public par un avis du Conservateur foncier du Wouri B daté du 27 octobre 2026. Autrement dit, vingt ans de vie juridique, vingt ans d’actes, de ventes, de constructions, de projets, de mariages célébrés sur une parcelle, d’enfants nés sur une terre, balayés en une phrase administrative. La haute juridiction a annulé le jugement du Tribunal administratif du Littoral du 17 décembre 2020, qui avait déjà interprété une décision de novembre 2018 défavorable au titre. Le ministère des Domaines, du Cadastre et des Affaires foncières, loin de protéger les citoyens, a autorisé l’exécution par courrier du 22 juillet 2025. L’État, à la fois juge, partie et bourreau. Le titre couvrait plus de 278 hectares au lieu-dit Japoma, à Douala 3e. Un certificat de propriété, délivré le 2 novembre 2026 à la demande de Moïse Herbert Zanga, confirme l’annulation. La liste des titres parcellaires visés approche les 800 numéros. Leurs copies sont déclarées « nulles et de nul effet ». Voilà la réalité : près de 800 familles, 800 acquéreurs de bonne foi, 800 détenteurs qui ont payé, notarié, construit, sont désormais des occupants sans droit. Qui les indemnisera ? Qui répondra de cette insécurité juridique organisée par l’État lui-même ? Car c’est là le scandale. Le titre foncier, au Cameroun, est censé être inattaquable, définitif, la garantie suprême de la propriété. Que vaut-il désormais, si l’État peut le délivrer, laisser prospérer un quartier entier, puis l’annuler vingt ans plus tard sans la moindre protection pour les victimes ? À Japoma, ce n’est pas une simple décision de justice. C’est la démonstration d’un État qui fabrique l’insécurité foncière, qui joue avec la terre des autochtones comme avec celle des acquéreurs, et qui abandonne ses citoyens au chaos. Quand l’État lui-même détruit la confiance dans le titre foncier, que reste-t-il du droit de propriété ? Cet article Japoma : le titre foncier en mode loterie d'Etat est apparu en premier sur Journalducameroun.com .

items.title: Pakistani farmers in long fight to make German firms pay for 2022 flood damage
items.description: In a village nestled in rice fields, Abdul Hafeez Khoso remembers the vast industrial zones he saw in Germany when he visited to file a pioneering climate legal case. “They’re spreading pollution: up in the sky there are no borders, it can affect anywhere,” the 43-year-old said, describing areas far larger than his village of 800 people. “This is a problem for the whole world — that is why it should be resolved at the global level.” Khoso and 38 other farmers from Sindh who were devastated by “apocalyptic” flooding in 2022 are suing German energy firm RWE and cement maker Heidelberg Materials in a rare bid to make big polluters pay damages for climate impacts. The companies are being targeted not over specific operations in Pakistan, but because of their climate-warming emissions . They are headquartered in Germany, where a recent legal case opened the door to such suits. The litigation argues that the companies’ emissions contributed to climate change and turbo-charged rain that wiped out their crops, livestock and homes. “The year 2022 was an apocalyptic scene — not even our elders had ever witnessed such weather,” Khoso, who lives in the district of Jacobabad with his wife and toddler, told AFP . “We had nothing left.” This photograph taken on July 29, 2026 shows Abdul Hafeez Khoso (C), one of the 39 farmers pursuing a climate lawsuit in Heidelberg for climate-warming emissions and over losses incurred during the 2022 floods, speaking with villagers at Jacobabad in Sindh. — AFP Both firms, which the plaintiffs estimate contributed 0.68 per cent and 0.12pc to global industrial emissions respectively, deny wrongdoing. Khoso’s case is backed by Pakistani and European organisations hoping to win compensation and build on nascent but vigorous international efforts to extract climate damages from corporations. “We always blame natural disasters, and sometimes we blame God, but science tells us that climate change is increasing the risks and intensity of extreme weather events,” said Mir Keerio, a development expert at HANDS Welfare Foundation, which mobilised communities for the lawsuit. “Those who have contributed significantly to this crisis must be held accountable … we realised we must take our fight for climate justice to the major polluters.” Debt and damages Climate litigation is a growing field globally, but action has so far largely targeted governments, with only a handful of firms such as Shell and cement maker Holcim facing suits for climate disaster compensations. Lawyers say a ruling requiring a company to pay out compensation proportionate to its greenhouse gas emissions would mark a major breakthrough. Germany’s judiciary moved towards that principle last year in a case brought by a Peruvian farmer, also against RWE. His compensation claim was rejected, but the courts left the door open to holding emitters liable. Roda Verheyen, a German lawyer involved in both cases, told AFP the farmers’ lawsuit builds on that ruling and further accuses companies of “wrongful behaviour”. “Large companies knew about the general impacts of climate change since the 1960s,” said Verheyen. “They should have exercised due diligence and actually at least tried to reduce emissions, which they didn’t do enough.” The lawsuit also draws on research documenting farmers’ losses in the floods, which hit a third of the country, killed 1,700 and affected 30 million. Munawar Khatoon, a rare female landowner in a conservative area, said the floods struck just before the wheat harvest, submerging seeds and wiping out her family’s main source of income. “We worry about how the next generation will manage to live if this continues,” the 43-year-old told AFP in her village Usman Samtio. “Now when the rainy season comes, we feel fear.” In nearby Dadu district, litigant Abdul Khalique Laghari said the floods affected the region for years. This photograph taken on July 27, 2026 shows Abdul Khalique Laghari (R), one of the 39 farmers pursuing a climate lawsuit in Heidelberg for climate-warming emissions and over losses incurred during the 2022 floods, walking across his agricultural field at Baid Sharif village in Dadu district. — AFP “To this day, we are unable to repay our debt,” said the 55-year-old, who estimates he lost $14,000 in assets including his house, 40 acres (16 hectares) of crops and livestock. “When we wake in the morning, we start getting calls from the people we owe money to,” he said, pointing to crumbling walls and the remnants of flood-damaged houses. “This has caused us serious mental harm.” ‘For justice’ RWE and Heidelberg Materials both call the claims in the suit “unfounded”. Heidelberg Materials told AFP its operations were compliant with German laws and that firms could not be expected to retroactively face different standards. RWE referred AFP to a statement describing the lawsuit as “yet another attempt to shift climate policy demands to German courtrooms”. “It would be a contradiction in terms if the state allowed CO2 emissions, regulated them by law and even demanded them in some cases, but at the same time allowed retroactive civil liability for them,” it said. Even if the case succeeds, an uphill battle remains for millions across Pakistan, ranked among the countries most affected by climate change despite contributing less than one per cent of global emissions. The case will be considered in a civil process likely to take years. But for the litigants, the attempt is worth it. “This case is for justice,” said Khatoon. “We hold these companies responsible for our destruction.” Header image: This photograph taken on July 27, 2026 shows Gul Hassan Babar, one of the 39 farmers pursuing a climate lawsuit in Heidelberg against German energy firm RWE and cement producer Heidelberg Material for climate-warming emissions and over losses incurred during the 2022 floods, walking across his agricultural field at Baid Sharif village in Dadu district. — AFP

items.title: Kouremalé prépare le retour des orpailleurs burkinabè
items.description: © Internet Ouagadougou a mobilisé une centaine de bus après l’afflux venu de Guinée. La prise en charge sanitaire fait apparaître plusieurs décès et une centaine de patients. Une délégation gouvernementale burkinabè a rencontré le ministre malien de la Sécurité, Daoud Aly Mohammedine, le 4 novembre à Bamako. Elle était conduite par le ministre burkinabè de la Sécurité, Mahamadou Sana, accompagné de la ministre chargée de la Famille et de la Solidarité, Passowendé Pélagie Kaboré. La réunion a porté sur l’accueil des ressortissants burkinabè arrivés au Mali après leur départ des sites aurifères de Siguiri, en Guinée, et sur leur acheminement vers le Burkina Faso. Les deux parties ont convenu d’organiser le transport en coordination avec l’ambassade burkinabè et les services maliens présents à Kouremalé. Mahamadou Sana a annoncé la mobilisation d’une centaine de bus. Cinquante étaient en route vers le Mali au moment de sa déclaration et le début de l’opération était annoncé pour jeudi 5 novembre. Des sites d’accueil ont également été identifiés au Burkina Faso avant le retour des personnes concernées dans leurs familles. Deux bilans humains communiqués Le Centre de santé communautaire de Kouremalé a enregistré quatre décès parmi les personnes arrivées de Guinée. Environ cent malades et blessés y étaient pris en charge le 5 novembre. Certains présentaient des blessures par balle, selon le responsable de la structure cité par l’Agence malienne de presse. Ramdé Antoine, premier conseiller à l’ambassade du Burkina Faso au Mali, a avancé pour sa part un bilan de neuf morts. Des représentants burkinabè ont estimé à plus de 40 000 le nombre de leurs compatriotes concernés. Ce chiffre correspond à une estimation communiquée lors de la réunion locale du 4 novembre. Les autorités guinéennes présentent leurs opérations à Siguiri comme une campagne contre l’orpaillage anarchique et illégal. Les mesures annoncées comprennent le contrôle des identités et des conditions de séjour sur les sites miniers. Le gouvernement guinéen invoque la protection de l’environnement, des terres agricoles et des cours d’eau. Les affirmations faisant état de tirs et de départs forcés proviennent du maire de Benkadi et de responsables burkinabè. La présence de personnes atteintes par balle a été rapportée par le centre de santé, tandis que les circonstances de ces blessures demandent encore une documentation indépendante. À Kouremalé, les services sanitaires, sociaux, sécuritaires et les transporteurs participent à l’accueil. Plusieurs centaines de personnes avaient déjà quitté la localité pour d’autres communes du cercle de Kangaba avant le lancement annoncé du transport vers le Burkina Faso. Massiré Diop

items.title: Niobium de Mabounié : DUSK soumet au gouvernement son projet de plus de 2 milliards de dollars
items.description: DUSK Gabon a remis au gouvernement l’étude de faisabilité actualisée du gisement de Mabounié, dans le Moyen-Ogooué. La société vise une production annuelle de 16 000 tonnes de niobium à pleine capacité et prévoit de transformer le minerai au Gabon. Son projet comprend un parc industriel près de Port-Gentil. Pékin, le 6 novembre 2026. New Energy Metals et DUSK Gabon ont présenté au président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema leur étude sur l’exploitation du niobium de Mabounié. © D.R. Après plusieurs années de sommeil, le dossier minier de Mabounié revient devant les autorités gabonaises. Dans un communiqué daté du 9 novembre 2026, DUSK Gabon SA, filiale de la société émiratie New Energy Metals, annonce avoir achevé et transmis l’étude de faisabilité actualisée du projet. Selon l’entreprise, les résultats confirment sa viabilité technique et économique. L’investissement envisagé dépasse 2 milliards de dollars, soit plus de 1 170 milliards de francs CFA, et couvrirait la mine, le transport fluvial, les installations portuaires et les usines de traitement. Le niobium, utilisé notamment pour renforcer les aciers, occupe une place centrale dans le projet. DUSK vise une production d’environ 16 000 tonnes par an une fois les installations à pleine capacité. Le gisement renferme aussi du tantale et du titane, que la société prévoit de raffiner sur le sol gabonais. Elle estime qu’à terme, les métaux issus de Mabounié pourraient figurer parmi les principales exportations hors pétrole du pays. De la mine du Moyen-Ogooué à un parc industriel près de Port-Gentil L’étude de faisabilité actualisée reprend les travaux menés par le passé en modifiant plusieurs choix industriels. D’après Eric Tizon, directeur général de DUSK, les ingénieurs ont revu le plan d’exploitation de la mine et simplifié la logistique entre le gisement et le port. Le schéma retenu prévoit également l’aménagement d’un parc industriel près de Port-Gentil. Pour le Gabon, l’enjeu est de réaliser sur son territoire les opérations de traitement et de raffinage qui donnent au minerai une partie de sa valeur à l’exportation. DUSK indique avoir également revu le procédé de traitement pour récupérer davantage de métal à partir d’une même quantité de minerai et valoriser un plus grand nombre de métaux. «Ensemble, ces changements ont considérablemen t amélioré l’économie du projet» , affirme Eric Tizon. La société ne chiffre toutefois ni les gains de récupération ni leur incidence sur la rentabilité du projet. Le groupe chinois China ENFI Engineering Corporation assure l’essentiel des travaux d’ingénierie sur le traitement du minerai, les infrastructures et le raffinage du niobium, du tantale et du titane. Hatch, SRK Consulting, Mecater et CCCC First Harbor Engineering Company ont également contribué à l’étude. Quelques jours avant l’annonce de DUSK, le projet avait été évoqué en Chine, où le président Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema a reçu les dirigeants d’ENFI lors de sa visite d’État, selon la présidence gabonaise. Plus de 2 000 emplois prévus, un calendrier encore à préciser DUSK prévoit la création de plus de 2 000 emplois, sans préciser la répartition entre les postes liés au chantier et ceux qui seraient maintenus pendant l’exploitation. La société s’engage à privilégier le recrutement de Gabonais, à former des jeunes aux métiers de la mine et de la transformation et à faire appel aux entreprises locales. Elle dit également vouloir travailler avec les communautés riveraines et appliquer des normes environnementales et sociales internationales. Avec la remise de l’étude, le gouvernement dispose désormais du scénario industriel défendu par DUSK. La société se dit prête à engager la phase suivante avec les autorités et les communautés locales. Son communiqué ne précise toutefois ni la date d’une décision finale d’investissement ni celle du démarrage des travaux. L’article Niobium de Mabounié : DUSK soumet au gouvernement son projet de plus de 2 milliards de dollars est apparu en premier sur Gabonreview.com | Actualité du Gabon | .

items.title: Nvidia probes whether CEO Huang was target of foreign spying as he admits affair
items.description: Nvidia said on Monday its board was probing whether CEO Jensen Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, after a media report alleged he had a close relationship with a Chinese businesswoman who passed information to Beijing. Huang said in a message to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife and took “full responsibility” for his actions, while Nvidia said the CEO was committed to continuing to lead the company without interruption. The developments are likely to pressure the chipmaker’s stock, which has already fallen sharply amid worries about the AI boom’s sustainability, and may also raise questions about Huang’s future at the helm of the company he co-founded, analysts said. The New York Times reported last month that Huang had a relationship with Alice Huang, an unrelated former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, who US authorities investigated and concluded was a Chinese intelligence asset. US authorities have scrutinised Megaspeed, which buys AI chips from Nvidia, over suspicions it helped Beijing gain access to advanced AI chips that are barred from shipment to China. “The NVIDIA Board is initiating an independent investigation in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort. A committee of independent directors, assisted by outside independent counsel, will oversee the investigation,” Nvidia said. The company said on Sunday that while its board had no reason to believe that either US national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, its inquiry would examine all available information. The board has confidence in the CEO and his leadership team, Nvidia said, adding that Huang fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it. The developments have been met with ire in China, where the foreign ministry on Monday branded the reports “entirely baseless vilification and smearing”. US President Donald Trump said on Sunday he had not spoken to Huang about the allegations, but called him a fine person. “I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job,” he added. When asked if he believed he should have acted on intelligence when he was briefed about it, Trump said: “No, I don’t think so. I think he’s an honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.” The New York Times had reported that Trump was briefed about the intelligence findings roughly a year ago and chose not to do anything with the information. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declined to comment on Huang when asked by reporters earlier in the evening. Megaspeed did not respond immediately to a request for comment outside business hours. Huang said on Sunday that he was “committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security”. Huang admitted to having been unfaithful to his wife, saying, “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.” Addressing his colleagues, board, partners and shareholders, Huang said: “My responsibility is to serve you and be worthy of your trust. I have fallen short of that responsibility. I am fully committed to NVIDIA and will work to earn back your confidence.” China’s state-run Global Times questioned why the story had emerged soon after “the hard-won detente” between Beijing and Washington, following a meeting between the two countries’ presidents in September. “Is someone behind the scenes pushing an agenda and stirring up confrontation?” a Global Times editorial published on Monday asked. “If this logic of ‘presumed guilt’ is allowed to spread unchecked,” it warned, technology and trade exchanges would be hindered. But on the streets of Beijing, people interviewed by AFP were mostly unaware of Huang’s affair and expressed scepticism at claims that he was linked to a Chinese spy. One man surnamed Ma said that he did not think Huang’s affair was “a big deal”, doubting the incident would affect a potential meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit next week. Wen, a 56-year-old retiree, told AFP it was “a real shame” for Huang to have been caught cheating, as the entrepreneur is widely admired in China for his success in an “extremely critical” part of the tech industry. Piling pressure on Nvidia The investigation adds to pressure on Nvidia at a time investors are already pulling back amid uncertainty over the sustainability of the booming AI market that made the chipmaker one of the world’s most valuable companies. The $4.5 trillion chipmaker’s shares have given up all their gains this year amid a broader tech market rout triggered by worries over the pace of AI spending. Huang, who has led Nvidia for more than three decades, has been central to its rise to become a dominant supplier of AI chips. “There is clearly risk that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the Board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co. “This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock,” Ives said, adding that the news would also increase scrutiny about selling chips to China. In late October, Huang had told Bloomberg News that his relationship and interactions with Alice Huang were related to Megaspeed and were “completely normal and not unusual”. Josh Gilbert, lead analyst at trading platform eToro, said Huang’s fingerprints were on every part of the company’s rise, so any doubt over his position would matter to shareholders. “While the investigation is likely to dent sentiment, it won’t alter anything long-term unless it leads to a change at the top, at which point it becomes a completely different ball game,” Gilbert added. Top Republican lawmakers in the US House of Representatives had already called on Huang to brief Congress this month about the New York Times report. The report raises “significant national security concerns regarding [China’s] access to sensitive US technology and information”, the lawmakers said in a letter dated November 4. “It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk,” they added. US export controls since 2022 have sought to restrict China’s access to advanced Nvidia chips and the equipment needed to make them.

items.description: Dans le cadre du projet de co-organisation de la Coupe d’Afrique des Nations (CAN) 2030 par les pays membres de la Confédération des États du Sahel (AES), à savoir le Burkina Faso, le Mali et le Niger, la Camarade Ministre des sports,de la jeunesse et de l’emploi, Annick PIKBOUGOUM/ZINGUE OUATTARA a reçu, ce dimanche 8 novembre 2026, une mission d'évaluation de la Confédération africaine de football (CAF), conduite par Emmanuel Newton DASOBERI, Manager Professionnel de Football. L'équipe est venue faire le point de la visite au Camarade Ministre. Cette première visite d'évaluation a permis de passer en revue les éléments de base nécessaires à l'organisation d'une compétition de cette envergure, notamment les personnes-ressources, les infrastructures sportives et les établissements hôteliers. La mission a visité dans la journée du 8 novembre, le Stade du 4-Août, le Centre d'entraînement des Étalons (COMET) avec ses deux terrains et l'hôtel Lancaster Ouaga 2000. Cette visite a mobilisé les différentes composantes concernées, notamment les représentants de la primature, des ministères des affaires étrangères, de la construction de la patrie, de la santé, de la sécurité, des finances, de la culture, des membres fédéraux, du bureau national des grands projets, de Faso Mêbo et du Camarade SOMDAH Toussaint, expert indépendant. Cette évaluation constitue une première étape et d'autres missions d'experts de la CAF sont attendues, notamment dans les domaines de la sécurité, des technologies de l'information, des infrastructures et commodités, ainsi que de la santé. Ces différentes évaluations permettront d'examiner progressivement les capacités et les dispositions des pays candidats, en collaboration avec le Mali et le Niger. La Camarade Ministre a traduit la ferme volonté du gouvernement du Burkina Faso et celui de l'AES à pouvoir constituer un dossier solide à même de recueillir l'autorisation de la CAF pour organiser la CAN 2030 pour le bonheur de la population de l'espace AES. DCRP/MSJE

items.title: Makokou : deux mois après les inaugurations, les malfaçons rattrapent les chantiers présidentiels
items.description: Deux mois après les festivités du 30 août, plusieurs infrastructures inaugurées dans la capitale provinciale de l’Ogooué-Ivindo font l’objet de réserves. Au terme d’une inspection menée le 5 novembre sur instruction du chef de l’État, Melodie Jennyfer Sambat annonce un rapport circonstancié et des mesures correctives assorties d’échéances. Melodie Jennyfer Sambat, conseillère spéciale chargée de mission du président de la République, au marché municipal de Makokou. © D.R. Inaugurer ne suffit pas, encore faut-il que les infrastructures soient effectivement fonctionnelles et répondent aux besoins des populations. C’est le message porté par Melodie Jennyfer Sambat, conseillère spéciale chargée de mission du président de la République, Brice Clotaire Oligui Nguema, à l’issue d’une mission de suivi effectuée le jeudi 5 novembre 2026 à Makokou. Conduite sur instruction du chef de l’État, cette inspection visait à évaluer les réalisations présentées lors des festivités de la Fête de la Libération du 30 août dernier. Accompagnée du gouverneur de l’Ogooué-Ivindo, du préfet de l’Ivindo, des représentants de la mairie, des forces de défense et de sécurité ainsi que des services de l’État, la délégation a passé en revue sept sites : le marché municipal, les logements de Maïga, l’aire de jeux de la place des fêtes, l’immeuble administratif, l’immeuble BCEG, l’hôtel Ivindo Palace et le lycée Alexandre Sambat. Des réserves et des engagements de correction A Makokou, un marché municipal presque vide et des bâtiments administratifs pleins de malfaçons découverts. © D.R. Au terme des visites, plusieurs insuffisances ont été relevées. Au marché municipal, des commerçantes ont notamment évoqué les difficultés à attirer la clientèle et la présence persistante de vendeuses exerçant à l'extérieur, malgré la disponibilité des nouveaux espaces commerciaux. Une concertation avec les autorités locales et les forces de sécurité est envisagée pour améliorer l'organisation et l'occupation du site. Des défauts de finition et des problèmes techniques ont également été signalés sur certains bâtiments, notamment des fissures au niveau de l'immeuble administratif et des travaux d'étanchéité à reprendre à l’immeuble BCEG. Les logements destinés aux officiers restent, quant à eux, annoncés comme devant être achevés en décembre. Pour Melodie Jennyfer Sambat, l'approche consiste à « regarder la réalité en face, écouter les responsables de chantier et les usagers, puis arrêter une solution et une échéance » . Des réserves ont ainsi été formulées et des engagements pris par les parties concernées, avec la promesse d'un suivi régulier jusqu'à la livraison effective des ouvrages. Un rapport attendu au sommet de l'État La mission entend désormais formaliser ses constats dans un rapport qui sera transmis au président de la République. Les entreprises concernées pourraient être appelées à reprendre les travaux présentant des défauts, tandis que les engagements pris devront faire l'objet d'un contrôle. « Inaugurer est un engagement. Mettre en service est une exigence » , a résumé la conseillère spéciale sur Facebook. Au-delà de la cérémonie officielle et de la livraison administrative, l'enjeu est donc désormais, selon la collaboratrice du chef de l’État, de garantir la qualité, la fonctionnalité et la durabilité des investissements réalisés à Makokou. Des infrastructures qui, selon elle, « appartiennent aux Ogivins » et doivent être mises au service de tous. items.title: L’électrification progresse quatre fois trop lentement pour atteindre l’objectif de la COP 31
items.description: La part de l’électricité dans la consommation finale d’énergie dans le monde a progressé de moins de 3 points en 10 ans, passant de 18,7 % en 2014 à 21,6 % en 2024, selon les données de l’Agence internationale de l’énergie. Si cette progression est régulière, elle est quatre fois trop lente pour atteindre l’objectif de 35 % d’ici 2035 que la présidence turque de la COP 31, qui s’ouvre aujourd’hui à Antalya, cherche à faire adopter. Cet indicateur est crucial pour la transition car l’électricité, qui est plus efficace que la combustion et sans émissions au point d’usage, couvre déjà près de 40 % des besoins en énergie utile – soit l’énergie disponible pour le chauffage, la climatisation ou l’éclairage. Dans un entretien à la revue, le directeur de l’Agence internationale de l’énergie, Fatih Birol, estime qu’en plus de l’impératif de diminution des émissions de CO₂, l’électrification répond également à un enjeu de souveraineté pour les pays et régions importateurs nets d’hydrocarbures. C’est notamment le cas de l’Europe : Birol dit être « convaincu que la souveraineté européenne dépend de notre capacité à électrifier nos économies. C’est une question de souveraineté, d’énergie et de compétitivité économique. C’est aussi, en définitive, la condition pour atteindre les objectifs climatiques ». Il ajoute : « Il faut souligner que l’Europe a progressé depuis le choc de 2022 en accélérant le déploiement des énergies renouvelables. Grâce à ces efforts considérables, les systèmes électriques européens ont été moins exposés aux perturbations de l’approvisionnement en gaz cette année qu’ils ne l’auraient été autrement. Mais il reste beaucoup à faire ». Selon une analyse de la revue, huit pays et territoires (Hong Kong, Islande, Norvège, Malte, Tadjikistan, Bahreïn, Taïwan et Israël) dépassaient déjà le seuil de 35 % en 2024. Sur les 150 pays et territoires étudiés, seulement deux ont électrifié leur économie au cours de la dernière décennie au rythme requis pour atteindre l’objectif mondial de 35 % d’ici 2035 : le Laos et le Venezuela 9 . Dans près des trois quarts des pays, le rythme d’électrification est inférieur à la moyenne mondiale de 0,31 point par an (62 pays), stagne (20 pays) ou recule (27 pays). Dans l’Union, l’Irlande (0,48 point par an) et le Luxembourg (0,34) sont les deux seuls États membres qui progressent à un rythme supérieur à la moyenne mondiale. La Chine a apporté en octobre son soutien à l’initiative portée par la Turquie China Backs Push for Global Electrification at UN Climate Talks », Bloomberg , 21 octobre 2026.'> 10 . Le pays affichait un taux d’électrification de 29,3 % en 2024, et devrait atteindre le seuil de 35 % dès 2030, soit cinq ans avant l’échéance, selon les prévisions de l’Administration nationale de l’énergie chinoise. Pékin reste toutefois de loin le premier émetteur mondial de gaz à effet de serre, et en a relâché dans l’atmosphère en 2024 davantage que les États-Unis et les 27 pays membres de l’Union réunis. L’article L’électrification progresse quatre fois trop lentement pour atteindre l’objectif de la COP 31 est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: Égypte: au moins 7 morts et 112 blessés dans un accident ferroviaire
items.description: Un grave accident ferroviaire s’est produit dans la soirée du dimanche 8 novembre 2026, à Gizeh, au sud du Caire, en Égypte. La collision entre deux trains a provoqué le déraillement de plusieurs wagons, faisant au moins sept morts et 112 blessés, selon les autorités égyptiennes, citées par des médias. D’après l’autorité ferroviaire égyptienne, un train en provenance de Gizeh et à destination de Fayoum a violemment percuté l’arrière d’un autre convoi qui reliait Le Caire à Assouan, dans le sud du pays. Le bilan communiqué par le ministère de la Santé fait état de sept passagers décédés et de 112 blessés. Parmi ces derniers, 88 étaient pris en charge dans différents établissements hospitaliers de la région de Gizeh, selon les premières informations disponibles. Informé du drame, le président égyptien, Abdel Fattah al-Sissi, a affirmé suivre la situation «avec une grande inquiétude». Il a également instruit les autorités compétentes d’ouvrir une enquête urgente afin d’établir les circonstances de l’accident et de «demander des comptes à toute personne dont la négligence serait avérée». Sur les lieux du drame, les équipes de secours ont été mobilisées pour les opérations de sauvetage et de dégagement des débris. Des grues ont notamment été utilisées pour extraire les épaves des wagons accidentés. Cette nouvelle catastrophe vient raviver les inquiétudes autour de la sécurité du réseau ferroviaire égyptien, régulièrement endeuillé par des accidents meurtriers. En 2002, un incendie survenu dans un train transportant des vacanciers, au sud du Caire, avait coûté la vie à plus de 370 personnes. En 2009, plusieurs collisions ferroviaires enregistrées dans cette même région avaient également fait des dizaines de victimes. Avec près de 110 millions d’habitants, l’Égypte dépend fortement du transport ferroviaire pour la mobilité de ses populations. Malgré son importance et son étendue, le réseau national continue ainsi d’être confronté à des accidents mortels à répétition, relançant la question de la sécurité des déplacements par train. Par Valentin SOMANDE L’article Égypte: au moins 7 morts et 112 blessés dans un accident ferroviaire est apparu en premier sur Wakat Séra .
